arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: The owner's counsel argued the state cannot compel speech. They stated the owner is a professional artist with free exercise rights.
The state's counsel argued Colorado extended protections to LGBTQ people. They noted the bakery is open to the public and subject to state law.
Justice Roberts questioned whether requiring a cake with a pre-existing message constitutes compelled association.
Justice Sotomayor questioned the scope of the refusal regarding standard items sold to the public.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on a bakery owner who refused to create a custom cake for a same-sex wedding. The state civil rights commission found this action violated anti-discrimination laws. The owner argues this requirement forces him to express a message he opposes. The state argues the law protects customers from discrimination based on sexual orientation.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The bakery owner wants the court to strike down the commission's order. He seeks a ruling that allows him to refuse service based on religious beliefs.
The state commission wants the court to uphold the anti-discrimination finding. It seeks to enforce the law requiring businesses to serve all customers equally.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The owner argues the First Amendment prohibits the government from forcing him to create expressive art. He claims making the cake violates his religious convictions about marriage.
The state argues the anti-discrimination law protects customers from bias. It asserts the owner must serve all shoppers regardless of their sexual orientation or the event type.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between religious freedom and anti-discrimination law. It determines whether businesses can refuse service based on the customer's identity. The outcome shapes how states enforce civil rights protections for LGBTQ individuals. It also clarifies the scope of free speech rights for commercial artists.
